newsitem.title: USA: Philippine peso move preempted trouble - US analysts.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso move preempted trouble - US analysts.

text.p: The Philippines' de facto currency devaluation on Friday should free the country from trouble down the road, U.S. investors said Friday.
The Philippine central bank's move Friday to widen the peso's target range against the dollar did not surprise analysts here, who said it would forestall market pressures.
"It's a good move by the central bank because it would avoid costly, protracted intervention action," said Feroz Talyarkhan, managing director at Bear Stearns.
"The main thing is to do away with the volatility, and if that means weakening your currency, so be it," he added.
Bankers had estimated the central bank had spent up to $2.0 billion to fight off currency speculators after last week's effective devaluation of the Thai baht.
Philippine policymakers had repeatedly denied in recent weeks that they were considering a devaluation.
The peso dropped 11.5 percent after the announcement, falling to 29.45 per dollar, the lowest level in four years. Trading was halted after it moved beyond a 1.5 percent reference rate.
"In the medium term, a freer exchange-rate regime will be positive for the Philippines," said Susan Gray, portfolio manager at Scudder, Stevens & Clark.
U.S. analysts described the Philippine situation as free from the macroeconomic imbalances that forced Thailand to devalue, but they applauded Friday's move.

"It's bitter medicine, but it's better to do now before things got out of whack," said one analyst at a major U.S. mutual fund. "My sense is that it's not going to take away from the overall good picture."
Standard and Poor's currently maintains a positive outlook on the Philippines BB-plus long-term foreign currency rating, while Moody's Investors Service holds the rating at Ba1.

The analyst forecast that the Philippines would win an upgrade to investment-grade status in 1998. He also predicted the peso would stabilize next week in a trading range of about 29-30 to the dollar.
Talkyarkan estimated that peso rate would trade in a range of 27.3-27.7 per dollar once the voilatility lets up, but suggested that the 29 pesos might hold over the coming week.

Philippine Brady bonds trailed the broader market but did not suffer much the central bank move, as the country's FLBS-A widened five basis points to 93-7/8 and Pars lost 13 basis points to 88-3/8, traders said.

Scudder's Gray said that Phillipines insitutitons had seemed willing to hold onto the dollar denominated Bradies amid a climate of uncertainty, and that international portfolio managers had weathered the storm.
"I believe foreign investors who may have held the Philippines are fairly comfortable with the Philippines fundamentals as an improving story," Gray said.
